block.prompt:
Not everyone agrees that the answer is fewer visitors. Listen twice to Daniel Reisz, who runs bus tours to the region, and then answer the questions below in full sentences.

[Your teacher reads:]
Daniel: “Honestly? I think this whole ‚overtourism' panic is exaggerated. For eight months of the year these villages are half empty and desperate for customers. The crowding lasts a few weeks in summer. We don't close a motorway because it's busy on a Friday evening — we manage it. Spread the visitors across the year, book time slots, put the money from tickets back into the village, and the problem mostly disappears. What I hear from some campaigners sounds less like a real transport problem and more like they simply don't want to share their beautiful home.”

(a) What is Daniel's overall attitude towards the idea of “overtourism”? Quote two or three words that show it.
(b) Daniel makes a comparison to explain his point. What does he compare the busy villages to, and what is that comparison meant to suggest?
(c) Pick ONE thing Daniel says that is a fact and ONE that is his opinion. How can you tell the difference?
(d) Look at his final sentence. What is he suggesting about the real motives of some campaigners?
block.answer_key: (a) He thinks it is overstated / not a real crisis: “exaggerated”, “panic”. (b) He compares the villages to a motorway that is busy on a Friday evening: just as you manage a busy road instead of closing it, you should manage peak tourist times instead of cutting visitor numbers — the crowding is a manageable peak, not a reason to turn people away. (c) FACT (checkable): e.g. “for eight months of the year these villages are half empty” / “the crowding lasts a few weeks in summer”. OPINION (a judgement): e.g. “the panic is exaggerated” / campaigners “don't want to share their beautiful home”. A fact can in principle be measured or checked; an opinion expresses a personal evaluation. (d) He implies their concern is not really about crowd management at all but about selfishness — that they simply don't want to share the place with outsiders.
block.acceptable_reasoning: Für (c) sind verschiedene Zuordnungen zulässig, solange die Begründung stimmt (überprüfbar vs. wertend). Für (d) zählt jede Antwort, die den unterstellten Vorwurf (Egoismus / ‚nicht teilen wollen') erkennt.

levels: Attitude named precisely and supported with the right words
Attitude broadly correct but weakly evidenced
Only literal content restated; attitude not identified
Clear example of each with a correct, explained distinction
Full, mostly accurate sentences; ideas clear
Understandable with errors that do not block meaning

watch_outs: ‚analyze' heißt: über das Wörtliche hinausgehen. Manche Schüler:innen fassen Daniel nur zusammen, statt seine HALTUNG zu benennen — gezielt nach den wertenden Wörtern fragen.
Der Motorway-Vergleich (b) wird oft wörtlich genommen (‚er redet über Autobahnen'). Die übertragene Bedeutung (Spitzen managen statt sperren) einfordern.
Fakt/Meinung (c): ‚half empty for eight months' klingt für manche wie eine Meinung — klarmachen, dass es prinzipiell messbar und damit ein (behaupteter) Fakt ist.
